{{Short description|Graded lattice with modular maximal chain}}
In mathematics, a '''supersolvable lattice''' is a [[graded poset|graded]] [[Lattice (order)|lattice]] that has a maximal [[total order#Chains|chain]] of elements, each of which obeys a certain modularity relationship. The definition encapsulates many of the nice properties of [[lattice of subgroups|lattices of subgroups]] of [[supersolvable group]]s.

==Motivation==
A finite [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> is said to be ''supersolvable'' if it admits a maximal [[subgroup series|chain (or ''series'') of subgroups]] so that each subgroup in the chain is normal in <math>G</math>.  A normal subgroup has been known since the 1940s to be left and (dual) right [[Modular pair|modular]] as an element of the lattice of subgroups.<ref>{{harvtxt|Schmidt|1994|loc=Theorem 2.1.3 and surrounding discussion}}</ref>  [[Richard P. Stanley|Richard Stanley]] noticed in the 1970s that certain [[geometric lattice]]s, such as the [[partition lattice]], obeyed similar properties, and gave a lattice-theoretic abstraction.<ref name="origpaper">{{harvtxt|Stanley|1972}}</ref><ref name="sternexamples"/>

==Definition==
A finite graded lattice <math>L</math> is '''supersolvable''' if it admits a maximal chain <math>\mathbf{m}</math> of elements (called an '''M-chain''' or '''chief chain''') obeying any of the following equivalent properties.

# For any chain <math>\mathbf{c}</math> of elements, the smallest sublattice of <math>L</math> containing all the elements of <math>\mathbf{m}</math> and <math>\mathbf{c}</math> is distributive.<ref>{{harvtxt|Stern|1999|loc=Section 4.3}}</ref>  This is the original condition of Stanley.<ref name="origpaper"/>
# Every element of <math>\mathbf{m}</math> is [[modular lattice#Modular pairs and related notions |left modular]]. That is, for each <math>m</math> in <math>\mathbf{m}</math> and each <math>x \leq y</math> in <math>L</math>, we have <math>(x\vee m)\wedge y=x\vee(m\wedge y).</math><ref>{{harvtxt|Stern|1999|loc=Corollary 4.3.3}} (for semimodular lattices)</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|McNamara|Thomas|2006|loc=Theorem 1}}</ref>
# Every element of <math>\mathbf{m}</math> is rank modular, in the following sense: if <math>\rho</math> is the rank function of <math>L</math>, then for each <math>m</math> in <math>\mathbf{m}</math> and each <math>x</math> in <math>L</math>, we have <math>\rho(m\wedge x)+\rho(m\vee x)=\rho(m)+\rho(x).</math><ref>{{harvtxt|Stanley|2007|loc=Proposition 4.10}} (for geometric lattices)</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Foldes|Woodroofe|2021|loc=Theorem 1.4}}</ref>

For comparison, a finite lattice is geometric if and only if it is [[atom (order theory)|atomistic]] and the elements of the [[antichain]] of atoms are all left modular.<ref>{{harvtxt|Stern|1999|loc=Theorems 1.72 and 1.73}}</ref>

An extension of the definition is that of a '''left modular lattice''': a not-necessarily graded lattice with a maximal chain consisting of left modular elements. Thus, a left modular lattice requires the condition of (2), but relaxes the requirement of gradedness.<ref>{{harvtxt|McNamara|Thomas|2006}}</ref>

==Examples==
[[File:Noncrossing partitions 4; Hasse.svg|thumb|[[Hasse diagram]] of the [[noncrossing partition]] lattice on a 4 element set.  The leftmost maximal chain is a chief chain.]]

A group is supersolvable if and only if its lattice of subgroups is supersolvable.  A [[chief series]] of subgroups forms a chief chain in the lattice of subgroups.<ref name="sternexamples">{{harvtxt|Stern|1999|p=162}}</ref>

The partition lattice of a finite set is supersolvable.  A partition is left modular in this lattice if and only if it has at most one non-[[singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] part;<ref name="sternexamples"/> thus, the partition lattice is also geometric.<ref>{{harvtxt|Stanley|2007|loc=Example 4.11}}</ref>  The [[noncrossing partition]] lattice is similarly supersolvable,<ref>{{harvtxt|Heller|Schwer|2018}}</ref> although it is not geometric.<ref>{{harvtxt|Simion|2000|p=370}}</ref>

The lattice of flats of the [[graphic matroid]] for a [[undirected graph|graph]] is supersolvable if and only if the graph is [[chordal graph|chordal]].  Working from the top, the chief chain is obtained by removing vertices in a [[perfect elimination ordering]] one by one.<ref>{{harvtxt|Stanley|2007|loc=Corollary 4.10}}</ref>

Every [[modular lattice]] is supersolvable, as every element in such a lattice is left modular and rank modular.<ref name="sternexamples"/>

==Properties==
A finite [[matroid]] with a supersolvable lattice of flats (equivalently, a lattice that is both geometric and supersolvable) has a real-rooted [[matroid#Polynomial invariants|characteristic polynomial]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Sagan|1999|loc=Section 6}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Stanley|2007|loc=Corollary 4.9}}</ref>  This is a consequence of a more general factorization theorem for characteristic polynomials over modular elements.<ref>{{harvtxt|Stanley|2007|loc=Theorem 4.13}}</ref>

The [[Arrangement of hyperplanes#The Orlik–Solomon algebra |Orlik-Solomon algebra]] of an [[arrangement of hyperplanes]] with a supersolvable intersection lattice is a [[Koszul algebra]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Yuzvinsky|2001|loc=Section 6.3}} </ref>  For more information, see [[Supersolvable arrangement]].

Any finite supersolvable lattice has an [[edge lexicographic labeling]] (or EL-labeling), hence its [[order complex]] is [[shelling (topology)|shellable]] and [[Cohen-Macaulay]].  Indeed, supersolvable lattices can be characterized in terms of edge lexicographic labelings: a finite lattice of height <math>n</math> is supersolvable if and only if it has an edge lexicographic labeling that assigns to each maximal chain a permutation of <math>\{ 1, \dots, n\}.</math><ref>{{harvtxt|McNamara|Thomas|2006|p=101}}</ref>
